meaning_fix: connections / pull (influence used to get something done)
reasoning: Emphatic ط as T, taa marbuta as a after it. Literally a means or intermediary, but in Ramallah waasTa almost always means the personal connections you pull to get a job or a permit.
ذ in this inherited word merges with د in Ramallah, as in dahab 'gold', so ذهبي is respelled دَهَبِي. The nisba ending is a short -i.
Long aa in the first syllable, then a short i before the cluster: shaawirma, ending in a long a. Turkish loan used everywhere in Ramallah.
Form II participle with the initial vowel dropped; the shadda doubles ق, which is a glottal stop, hence the two apostrophes, and ط is T.
From French culotte, borrowed with a short i and long uu: kiluut. The everyday Ramallah word for underpants.
b-imperfect of bayyan with shadda on ي: bibayyin, 'it appears'. inno is the Palestinian complementiser; mbayyan inno is an equally common variant.

meaning_fix: 'five and a little five', said to ward off the evil eye (also the hamsa / hand of Fatima)
reasoning: Taa marbuta after س is e in both words: khamse w khamiise. It is primarily the spoken charm said when someone praises you, and by extension the hand amulet.
Stative verbs of this class take the CiCiC shape in Palestinian: firi7, not MSA fari7a. ح is 7.
Emphatic ط as T, and its emphasis backs the final vowel, so the taa marbuta is a. Used in Ramallah, though mi'laaye is the commoner word for a frying pan.
In this learned word ذ surfaces as plain z in urban Palestinian, so I respell ذاكرة as زَاكِرَة for the voice. Taa marbuta after ر is a.
ذ merges with د in this inherited religious word, and the cluster is broken by a helping vowel: nidir, as in 3alayy nidir. I am less sure whether some Ramallah speakers keep nadr.
ث is t, and the hundreds compound with miyye: tultumiyye, taa marbuta as e after ي. tlatmiyye is also heard in Ramallah.
Built on mushkile with the Turkish agent suffix -ji. The vowels vary between speakers, which is why confidence is low; the sense 'troublemaker' is solid.
Emphatic ص as S, the shadda doubling ح to 77, then the dual ending -een: Sa77teen, literally 'two healths'. Said before or during a meal.
3een has ee, with the first person -i. The feminine colour adjective ends in a long a: 7amra.
haada plus the article contracts to hal-, giving shu hal-7alaawe. Taa marbuta after و is e, as in 'ahwe. Used to admire a person, a baby or a thing.
ق glottalises even in this administrative word: ta'aa3ud, with ع as 3. Heard in sinn it-ta'aa3ud, retirement age.
ح is 7 and the taa marbuta after م is e: 7ishme. Used in Ramallah mainly of modest dress and decorous behaviour.
Medial hamza written ', then long ii: ra'iis. Also 'boss / head' of an institution, not only a head of state.
The masculine pronoun is inte in Palestinian; word-initial hamza is written as the vowel. The set reply to tiSba7 3ala kheer, 'and may you be of its people'.
Italian-French loan with two long oo vowels. Understood in Ramallah but it has a Lebanese flavour; for a main road Palestinians more often say ish-shaari3 ir-ra'iisi.
Palestinian makes passives with it- plus the Form II stem: itSalla7, emphatic ص doubled whole by the shadda on ل.
ظ is written TH per the scheme, doubled by the shadda; Ramallah speakers say it as an emphatic z. Taa marbuta after م is e. Thoroughly everyday, as in munaTHTHamet it-ta7riir.
CiCiC past in Palestinian: rikib, not MSA rakiba. Used for getting into a car or onto a bus as well as riding.
ishi 'thing' is a distinctly Palestinian word. The hamza is written after the article prefix, as in il-'usbuu3, so il-'ishi; nafs means 'the same'.
